readings.title: The Box by the Door
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: On the first evening in her new apartment, Emi put a small wooden box beside the door. Her grandfather had given it to her with a note: “A place for things that are going somewhere.” She assumed he meant keys. However, when she visited him the following Sunday, she noticed that his keys hung on a hook. His own box contained a library book, an empty jam jar, and a folded shopping bag.

The objects were waiting for different journeys. The book had to be returned, the jar belonged to a neighbor, and the bag was needed for shopping. Her grandfather explained that he used to put such things away neatly and then forget to take them out. Keeping everything visible made the room less tidy, but it saved him several unnecessary trips.

Emi tried the idea. She placed a form for her new school in the box, along with a scarf she had borrowed. The next morning, she remembered both. A week later, however, the box was full of advertisements, old receipts, and objects with no clear destination. It had become another place where she left things instead of deciding what to do with them.

She called her grandfather, who laughed and admitted that the same thing happened to him. His solution was to empty the box every Friday and ask where each item needed to go. Emi chose Sunday evening instead. She kept the scarf there until she arranged to meet its owner, but threw away the advertisements immediately. The box did not organize her life for her. It gave her a visible reminder, provided that she occasionally stopped to make the decisions it could not make.

questions.prompt: What was the grandfather’s box mainly used for?
choices: Protecting valuable objects from visitors.
Keeping items ready for a future action outside the home.
Storing objects that would never be used again.
Separating new possessions from old ones.
questions.explanationJa: 本の返却や借り物の返還など、次に外へ持っていく物を見える場所に置く箱でした。

evidence.quote: The objects were waiting for different journeys

questions.prompt: Why had putting these objects away neatly caused a problem?
choices: The objects were damaged when they were hidden.
The apartment had too little storage space.
The grandfather could not remember who owned them.
He sometimes forgot to take them with him.
questions.explanationJa: きちんと片付けると、外出時に取り出すことを忘れ、余分な往復が必要になっていました。

evidence.quote: put such things away neatly and then forget to take them out

questions.prompt: What went wrong when Emi first used the box?
choices: She began putting things there without deciding their next destination.
She returned borrowed objects before their owners needed them.
She followed her grandfather’s Friday routine too strictly.
She kept useful objects in too many different boxes.
questions.explanationJa: 持ち出す予定がある物だけでなく、判断を先送りした物まで入れるようになったことが問題でした。

evidence.quote: objects with no clear destination

Its main purpose was to make a room look perfectly tidy.

readings.title: Keeping an Object, Keeping a Story
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: When her father moved to a smaller apartment, Nao helped sort the contents of his study. They agreed easily about broken pens and outdated calendars. A worn wooden ruler produced a longer conversation. It no longer had clear markings, and a newer ruler lay beside it. Nao put the old one in the box for disposal. Her father took it out again.

The ruler had belonged to his older sister, who had taught him to draw simple building plans when they were children. He did not need it for measuring. Its value came from the particular person and period it brought to mind. Nao understood this explanation, but there were several cupboards of objects with stories attached. The smaller apartment could not accommodate them all. Recognizing emotional value did not remove the practical need to choose.

Their first attempt to solve the problem was to photograph everything. This seemed to offer an efficient compromise: preserve the appearance while releasing the space. Yet the photographs were uneven substitutes. An image of a large school display captured almost everything her father wished to remember. A picture of the ruler did not convey its weight, the smooth place where his sister’s thumb had rested, or the experience of holding it while telling the story. Some memories were associated with an object’s physical qualities, not simply its visible form.

Nao began asking a different question. Instead of “Do you still need this?” she asked, “What would you want someone to understand about it?” The answer sometimes led to a short written account. Sometimes it suggested another person who might appreciate the object. A collection of teaching materials went to a former colleague who could use it, while a small group of personal items stayed with her father. The decision was not based on a general rule that useful objects should remain and sentimental ones should go. Different objects supported different kinds of continuity.

There were also disagreements they could not immediately resolve. Nao worried that postponement would simply recreate the crowded cupboards. Her father worried that a rushed decision would be irreversible. They set aside one modest box for uncertain items and agreed to discuss it after the move. This was a limit rather than an unlimited permission to delay. It allowed them to finish the practical work without pretending that every attachment could be evaluated on demand.

The ruler eventually found a place on a small shelf. Several larger possessions did not make the move, although their stories were recorded. Nao had not discovered a universal method for reducing belongings. She had learned to distinguish between saving an object, saving information about it, and preserving a relationship through it. Those aims can overlap, but they are not identical. Thoughtful choices became possible when she stopped treating the objects as a single category of things that either occupied space or served a practical purpose.

questions.prompt: Why did Nao’s father retrieve the old ruler?
choices: He believed its remaining markings were more accurate than the newer ruler’s.
He expected his sister to need it for another building project.
It connected him to an experience that its practical condition did not explain.
It was the only object from his study that could fit in the new apartment.
questions.explanationJa: 定規としての実用性ではなく、姉と過ごした経験や記憶との結び付きに価値があったためです。

evidence.quote: Its value came from the particular person and period it brought to mind

questions.prompt: What limited the usefulness of photographs?
choices: They could not preserve every physical aspect associated with an object.
They required more storage space than the objects themselves.
They were helpful only for objects that had no personal significance.
They prevented the father from explaining why an object mattered.
questions.explanationJa: 写真は見た目を残せても、重さや手触り、実際に持つ感覚などは残せませんでした。

evidence.quote: Some memories were associated with an object’s physical qualities

questions.prompt: What purpose did the box for uncertain items serve?
choices: It allowed all difficult decisions to be avoided permanently.
It separated valuable possessions from objects intended for colleagues.
It ensured that the father would keep every item he initially wanted.
It provided a bounded delay for decisions that were difficult to make immediately.
questions.explanationJa: 保留できる量を限定することで、際限なく先送りせず、移転作業と気持ちの整理を両立させました。

evidence.quote: a limit rather than an unlimited permission to delay

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best reflects Nao’s experience?
choices: An object’s practical usefulness is the fairest measure of whether to keep it.
Different reasons for keeping possessions may call for different ways of preserving their value.
Recording the story of an object always removes the need to keep the object itself.
Emotional decisions should be postponed until practical limitations disappear.
questions.explanationJa: 物そのもの・情報・人とのつながりを残すことは同一ではなく、価値の種類に応じて残し方を考える必要があります。

evidence.quote: Those aims can overlap, but they are not identical

readings.title: The Answer Without the Method
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Daniel liked solving the short mathematics problems that his teacher put on the board each morning. He usually finished before his classmates. One day, Ms. Lee asked him to explain a solution to the class. Daniel wrote the correct answer immediately, but found it surprisingly difficult to explain how he had reached it. “I can see the pattern,” he said. That did not help a classmate who could not see it.

Ms. Lee gave the class three drawings showing the same number pattern in different ways. Working with a partner, Daniel had to identify what remained unchanged. His partner, Mina, was slower at calculating but noticed a connection between the rows and the spaces between them. When she pointed to those spaces, Daniel suddenly found words for something he had previously recognized without explaining.

For homework, the students were asked to write a short explanation for someone who had missed the lesson. They were not allowed to begin with a formula. Daniel used a drawing first, followed by two examples. He then introduced the formula as a shorter way to describe what the examples had shown. Writing this took longer than his usual homework.

The next morning’s problem looked different from the earlier ones. Several numbers had been replaced by shapes. Daniel could not use the familiar pattern immediately. He returned to the relationship he and Mina had discussed, and worked out where to begin. He still enjoyed finding answers quickly. However, he now understood why his teacher sometimes asked students to slow down. Explaining a solution was not simply an extra task after the real work. It could reveal what made the solution work and help them recognize the same idea in an unfamiliar form.

questions.prompt: What difficulty did Daniel experience at the board?
choices: He had copied a number incorrectly from his notebook.
He could find the answer but could not make his thinking clear to others.
He had forgotten every number pattern from the previous lesson.
He disagreed with the answer that Ms. Lee expected.
questions.explanationJa: 正答はすぐ出せても、「パターンが分かる」以上の説明ができませんでした。

evidence.quote: found it surprisingly difficult to explain how he had reached it

questions.prompt: How did Mina help Daniel?
choices: She completed his homework while he practiced calculating.
She replaced the drawings with a formula from another lesson.
She showed him that all the drawings contained errors.
She identified a relationship that helped him describe his thinking.
questions.explanationJa: 列とその間の空間の関係を指摘し、Danielが言葉にできなかった理解を説明する助けになりました。

evidence.quote: Daniel suddenly found words for something he had previously recognized without explaining

questions.prompt: Why was the later problem important to Daniel’s learning?
choices: It showed that understanding a relationship could help when a problem looked unfamiliar.
It proved that using formulas was always slower than drawing pictures.
It demonstrated that speed was the only useful sign of understanding.
It allowed him to avoid thinking about the earlier lesson.
questions.explanationJa: 見た目が変わっても、本質的な関係を理解していれば解き始める手掛かりになると実感したためです。

evidence.quote: He returned to the relationship he and Mina had discussed

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why partners should always have the same calculation speed.
Why mathematics homework should avoid every kind of formula.
How explaining an answer can deepen understanding and make it more flexible.
How finishing first helps students give clearer explanations.
questions.explanationJa: 答えを説明することによって仕組みが見え、異なる見た目の問題にも理解を使えるようになるという話です。

evidence.quote: help them recognize the same idea in an unfamiliar form

readings.title: Learning to Read an Uncertain Document
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: In an imagined history seminar, students received three accounts of a fire at an old theater. One was a newspaper report written the next morning. Another was a letter composed by a performer several weeks later. The third was an interview recorded many years afterwards. The assignment appeared simple: reconstruct what had happened. Several students began by choosing the account they considered most trustworthy and using the others to fill in missing details.

Their teacher, Professor Hale, asked them to pause before deciding which source should dominate. The newspaper gave a precise starting time, but did not identify the person who supplied it. The performer’s letter described confusion backstage in vivid detail, yet its author had entered the building after the first alarm. The later interview explained why a particular exit was difficult to use, but confused the names of two people involved. Each source offered something useful while leaving different questions unresolved.

The students were accustomed to treating credibility as a single ranking: one source was reliable, another unreliable. This exercise required a more limited judgment. A witness might accurately describe what they saw in one room without knowing what happened elsewhere. A source close to an event could contain hurried assumptions, while a later account might incorporate information unavailable at the time. These possibilities did not make every account equally valuable. They made the value depend partly on the question being asked.

One student, Rosa, became frustrated when the group could not establish the exact minute at which the fire began. She felt that their work had failed to produce an answer. Hale asked whether the uncertainty affected every conclusion. The accounts disagreed about timing, but all described a delay before people at the rear of the building understood that they should leave. Rosa realized that she could state this shared observation while remaining cautious about the precise sequence. Her final reconstruction included both a narrative and a short explanation of where the evidence was insufficient.

The exercise also changed the students’ questions. Instead of asking only whether an author was honest, they considered the author’s position, access to information, purpose, and intended audience. The performer’s letter, for example, was written to reassure a worried parent. That purpose helped explain its emphasis, but did not automatically invalidate its details. Identifying a motive was a reason to investigate how a document was shaped, rather than an excuse to reject everything it contained.

By the end of the seminar, the class had produced several defensible reconstructions instead of a single perfectly certain account. Their differences were visible and open to challenge because claims were connected to specific evidence. The lesson was not that the past is unknowable or that any interpretation is acceptable. It was that careful reading involves calibrating the strength of a claim to the support available. Acknowledging a boundary in the evidence can make an explanation more informative, rather than less complete.

questions.prompt: Why did Hale ask the students not to choose one dominant source immediately?
choices: The oldest source was certain to contain the most serious mistakes.
Different sources could be useful for different parts of the reconstruction.
All three sources had been written for exactly the same audience.
Selecting a source would prevent them from writing a narrative at all.
questions.explanationJa: 各資料には得意な情報と限界があり、資料全体に一つの信頼順位を付けるだけでは十分でなかったためです。

evidence.quote: the value depend partly on the question being asked

questions.prompt: What did Rosa come to understand about the uncertain starting time?
choices: It meant that no conclusion about the event could be supported.
It could be established by ignoring the later interview.
It showed that the witnesses had deliberately concealed information.
It did not prevent her from identifying other observations supported by the accounts.
questions.explanationJa: 発生時刻が確定しなくても、後方の人々が避難を始めるまで遅れがあったという共通点は述べられました。

evidence.quote: she could state this shared observation while remaining cautious about the precise sequence

questions.prompt: How should the performer’s purpose in writing the letter be treated?
choices: As a factor that may shape the account and calls for closer examination.
As sufficient proof that every detail in the letter was invented.
As a reason to regard the letter as more precise than every other source.
As irrelevant because the author was personally involved in the event.
questions.explanationJa: 親を安心させる意図は記述の強調を左右しえますが、それだけで内容を全面否定する理由にはなりません。

evidence.quote: a reason to investigate how a document was shaped

questions.prompt: Which principle does the passage recommend?
choices: A convincing explanation should remove references to unresolved questions.
Disagreement among sources gives all interpretations equal merit.
The certainty of a conclusion should match the evidence supporting it.
Documents written soon after an event should always outweigh later accounts.
questions.explanationJa: 証拠が支えられる強さに合わせて主張の確かさを調整する、という読解原則を示しています。

evidence.quote: calibrating the strength of a claim to the support available

vocabulary.meaningJa: 無効にする・成立しなくする

readings.title: The Note on the Workshop Wall
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: On his first day helping at a furniture workshop, Luis was given a list of tasks. It explained where to store materials and how to record completed work. Beside the list, someone had written a strange instruction: “Before moving a chair, look at its feet.” Luis thought this was too obvious to need a reminder.

Later that morning, he carried a newly repaired chair toward the front room. A senior worker, Hana, stopped him. A small piece of red paper was attached to one leg. It meant that the glue had not yet been checked. The chair looked finished, but it was not ready for collection. Luis had read the task list carefully, yet the list had not explained the colored paper.

Hana showed him several other signals used around the workshop. A folded cloth marked a surface that needed protection. A card facing backward meant that someone was still checking the order. The workers understood these signs because they had used them for years. Hana realized that what seemed obvious to an experienced worker might be invisible to a newcomer.

That afternoon, Luis suggested adding photographs of the signs beside the written instructions. Hana agreed, but asked him to describe any other moments when he felt uncertain. By the end of the week, they had made a short guide called “Things We Forgot to Explain.” Luis still asked questions, and the guide did not replace training or careful supervision. However, it gave new workers a starting point and reminded experienced workers to explain their assumptions. The unusual note about the chair’s feet remained on the wall. Now it stood beside a photograph of the red paper and a clear explanation of what to do when it appeared.

questions.prompt: Why did Hana stop Luis from carrying the chair away?
choices: Its owner had canceled the collection.
One of its legs was missing.
A repair check had not yet been completed.
Luis had recorded it under the wrong customer’s name.
questions.explanationJa: 脚の赤い紙は接着剤の確認がまだ済んでいないことを示し、引き渡し準備が整っていませんでした。

evidence.quote: the glue had not yet been checked

questions.prompt: Why had the workers failed to explain the signs clearly?
choices: Their long experience made the meanings seem obvious to them.
They wanted newcomers to discover every rule through mistakes.
The signs changed too frequently to be included in a guide.
They believed photographs were less useful than written task lists.
questions.explanationJa: 長年使っていたため、経験者には当然の意味が新人には分からないことを見落としていました。

evidence.quote: they had used them for years

questions.prompt: What did Luis suggest adding to the instructions?
choices: A list of every customer’s preferred collection time.
A new schedule that removed repair checks.
Longer descriptions of the workshop’s history.
Photographs explaining the signals used at work.
questions.explanationJa: 日常的に使う目印の写真を、既存の説明のそばに加える提案でした。

evidence.quote: adding photographs of the signs beside the written instructions

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson of the story?
choices: Written instructions make supervision unnecessary for new workers.
Knowledge that experienced people take for granted may need to be made explicit.
New workers should avoid asking about simple-looking instructions.
Practical knowledge is useful only when it can be explained without pictures.
questions.explanationJa: 経験者が暗黙に知っていることを言葉や写真で見えるようにする重要性を描いています。

evidence.quote: reminded experienced workers to explain their assumptions

readings.title: The Craft of Knowing When to Ask
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: In a fictional restoration workshop, an apprentice named Sam was praised for working independently. He could prepare materials, follow a schedule, and complete familiar tasks without waiting for instructions. When an unfamiliar wooden frame arrived, he assumed that the same independence would be valued. A corner appeared slightly loose, so he began preparing the usual repair. His supervisor stopped him before he touched it.

The frame contained an earlier repair whose purpose was unclear. What looked like accidental damage might have reflected a deliberate adjustment, and changing it could erase information about the object’s history. Sam had followed a procedure he knew well, but had not recognized that the conditions for using it were uncertain. The supervisor’s concern was not simply whether he possessed the necessary hand skills. It was whether he understood when those skills should be applied and when further investigation was needed.

This distinction challenged Sam’s understanding of expertise. He had imagined progress as a gradual reduction in the number of questions he needed to ask. Experienced workers did ask fewer routine questions, but they did not ask none. Their questions became more selective. They could identify which details mattered, what assumptions a standard procedure depended on, and which consequences would be difficult to reverse. Independence consisted partly in recognizing the boundary of a decision, not merely in making it without assistance.

Over the following weeks, the supervisor asked Sam to explain his intended approach before starting unfamiliar work. The conversation was brief. He described what he knew, what he was assuming, and what might change his plan. At first, this felt like a return to constant checking. Gradually, however, he found that saying an assumption aloud sometimes exposed a gap before anyone else pointed it out. He also learned to distinguish uncertainty that could be resolved by inspecting the object from uncertainty requiring another person’s judgment.

The arrangement depended on how the supervisor responded. If every question had been treated as evidence of incompetence, Sam would have had an incentive to conceal doubt. Instead, she praised questions that identified a specific risk, while encouraging him to resolve familiar matters himself. This was not permission to transfer every decision upward. Asking a useful question required preparation: observing carefully, consulting existing records, and explaining why the available information was insufficient.

Months later, Sam received another frame with an unfamiliar joint. He did not immediately reach for the usual tools, nor did he simply wait for someone to tell him what to do. He examined the records and formulated a question about the joint’s purpose. His supervisor recognized this as progress. The episode suggests that professional development is not well described by a simple movement from dependence to complete self-sufficiency. Mature responsibility includes the ability to act, the ability to investigate, and the ability to recognize when collaboration is part of acting competently.

questions.prompt: What made the first frame different from Sam’s familiar tasks?
choices: It required materials that the workshop no longer stocked.
It had already been approved for the usual repair.
Its owner had requested that all earlier work be removed.
An earlier alteration had an uncertain purpose that might matter.
questions.explanationJa: 古い修理や調整が何のために行われたのか分からず、普通の損傷として直すと情報を失う恐れがありました。

evidence.quote: an earlier repair whose purpose was unclear

questions.prompt: How did Sam’s view of expertise change?
choices: He learned that experienced workers avoid decisions involving uncertainty.
He recognized that expertise includes identifying when a question is necessary.
He concluded that asking more questions always indicates greater skill.
He discovered that hand skills contribute little to restoration work.
questions.explanationJa: 熟練とは質問が不要になることではなく、前提や影響を見極めて必要な問いを立てられることだと理解しました。

evidence.quote: Their questions became more selective

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss the supervisor’s response to questions?
choices: To show that the apprentice’s uncertainty resulted mainly from unclear records.
To explain why supervisors should make every difficult decision themselves.
To show how workplace reactions can influence whether people reveal uncertainty.
To argue that preparation is unnecessary when help is available.
questions.explanationJa: 質問を無能の証拠として扱う職場では疑問を隠す動機が生まれるため、応答の仕方も重要だと説明しています。

evidence.quote: an incentive to conceal doubt

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage’s view of responsibility?
choices: Competent action may involve independent work, investigation, and well-judged collaboration.
Independence is achieved when a worker no longer needs to consult anyone.

questions.explanationJa: 責任ある行動には自力で進める力だけでなく、調査や適切な相談も含まれるという結論です。

evidence.quote: recognize when collaboration is part of acting competently

readings.title: Money for the Music Room
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: The music club at Eastbridge School wanted to replace its worn practice drums. At a meeting, the treasurer, Eva, announced that the club had collected enough money. Everyone was pleased until another member asked whether this included the money promised for next month’s concert. Eva checked her notebook. Almost half of the total came from ticket reservations that had not yet been paid for.

The club had also received a generous gift from a former student. However, the accompanying letter said that the money was intended for students who could not afford concert travel. It was in the same account as the club’s other funds, but the club had agreed to use it for that particular purpose. It could not simply be treated as money available for drums.

Eva reorganized her records into three sections: money already received and available, money expected later, and money set aside for a specific use. She also listed bills that would have to be paid before the concert. The account balance had not changed, but the amount that the club could safely spend immediately looked much smaller.

The members decided to borrow a drum set for the concert and review the purchase after ticket payments arrived. They also agreed to keep a small amount available for unexpected expenses. Eva was embarrassed about her earlier announcement, but the club leader thanked her for correcting it before placing an order. She had not lost any money. She had learned that a useful financial record must show more than a total. It must help people see when money will arrive, what commitments already exist, and which choices they are actually free to make.

questions.prompt: What was wrong with Eva’s first total?
choices: It included money expected from reservations that had not been paid.
It left out the cost of drums purchased several years earlier.
It counted every concert ticket payment twice.
It included only the former student’s gift.
questions.explanationJa: まだ入金されていないチケット予約分まで含めて、今使える金額のように考えていました。

evidence.quote: ticket reservations that had not yet been paid for

questions.prompt: Why was the former student’s gift not available for buying drums?
choices: The bank had refused to accept it.
The former student had requested repayment before the concert.
The club had accepted it for a different, specified purpose.

readings.title: The Same Total, Two Different Futures
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Two fictional neighborhood arts groups, Cedar and Willow, ended the year with the same amount in their accounts. Both had earned praise for successful exhibitions, and their annual summaries showed no unpaid bills. To a casual reader, their financial positions appeared almost identical. When they planned the following year, however, Cedar cautiously reduced its programme while Willow added a small exhibition. The difference was not explained by enthusiasm or artistic ambition.

Cedar’s balance included a large donation designated for repairing its exhibition building. The donor and the group had agreed on this purpose, and the roof work had not yet begun. Several workshops scheduled for the next season had also been paid for in advance. That cash was present, but the group still had to provide the promised activities. Treating the whole balance as freely available would have ignored commitments that did not appear as overdue bills.

Willow had fewer designated funds and had already paid most of its annual venue costs. Its incoming money was modest but arrived at regular intervals from membership payments. Cedar depended more heavily on a single fundraising event whose outcome varied substantially from year to year. Neither pattern was automatically better in every circumstance. A large event could support an ambitious project, while regular small payments could still decline. The important point was that equal balances concealed differences in timing, flexibility, and uncertainty.

The groups’ coordinators met to compare their plans. At first, Cedar’s coordinator described money kept for unexpected expenses as money doing nothing. Willow’s coordinator disagreed. The reserve did not purchase an exhibition immediately, but it reduced the likelihood that a delayed payment would force the cancellation of one already promised. Its purpose was not to eliminate every risk or to grow without limit. The amount had to be considered alongside the costs of postponing useful activities that the group could otherwise afford.

Their discussion also exposed a communication problem. A headline balance was easy to present to supporters, whereas a detailed account of future obligations required more explanation. Cedar worried that describing constraints would make a successful year sound disappointing. Yet failing to explain them could create expectations that the group could not meet. It decided to show available funds, committed funds, and expected income separately, with short notes about the assumptions behind its plans. The figures became less impressive at a glance but more useful for understanding actual choices.

The comparison illustrates the distinction between possessing money and having room to decide how to use it. Financial strength cannot be inferred from a single balance without considering what that money represents. Commitments, the timing of receipts, and the reliability of future income can change the meaning of the same total. For these groups, careful planning began not with choosing a universal target for savings, but with making their particular obligations and uncertainties visible to the people responsible for the next decision.

choices: One group had concealed unpaid bills from its annual summary.
Their members had different opinions about which art forms were most valuable.
The money represented different commitments and patterns of future income.
Both groups had received donations that could be spent without restriction.
questions.explanationJa: 使い道が決まった寄付や前払い済みのサービス、入金の安定性などが異なり、残高だけでは判断の余地を比較できませんでした。

readings.title: The Plant by the Window

paragraphs.text: For a school project, Nora compared two small plants. She put one beside a sunny window and another on a shelf farther away. After two weeks, the first plant was taller. Nora wrote that sunlight had caused it to grow faster. Before she finished her report, her brother asked how much water each plant had received.

Nora could not answer exactly. She had watered the window plant whenever its soil looked dry, but had sometimes forgotten the one on the shelf. The pots were different sizes, too. She had noticed a real difference in height, but several conditions had differed at the same time. Her observation alone could not tell her which condition explained the result.

For a second attempt, Nora chose similar plants in matching pots. She measured the water and kept notes about when it was added. She used more than one plant in each location, because a single plant might behave unusually. She also wrote down their heights before beginning. This time, she wanted to compare how much they grew, rather than simply which plants were tallest at the end.

The second project took more preparation and did not produce perfectly identical results within either group. Nora included those differences in her report instead of hiding them. She explained that her first attempt had suggested a question, while the second gave her a better way to investigate it. Her teacher praised this distinction. Nora had expected science to mean finding a clear answer quickly. She discovered that improving the question and noticing the limits of an answer could be important parts of the work.

readings.title: The Result That Refused to Repeat
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: A fictional school research team designed a simple device to measure how quickly water passed through different filters. In its first demonstration, a filter made from a new material appeared much faster than the familiar one. The students were excited. Their first draft described the new material as a clear improvement. Before submitting the work to an exhibition, they invited another class to repeat the procedure using their written instructions.

The second class did not obtain the same result. Its measurements were much closer together, and occasionally the familiar filter was faster. The original team initially suspected careless work. Yet when the two groups compared notes, they discovered that the instructions had omitted the amount of pressure applied while fitting each filter into the holder. One group pressed firmly; the other stopped as soon as the filter seemed secure. What had felt like an unimportant practical detail was potentially part of the experiment.

The discovery did not establish that fitting pressure explained the entire difference. Other possibilities remained, including variation between individual filters and the way the timing was started. The students resisted the temptation to replace one confident explanation with another. They listed the competing possibilities and changed one procedure at a time, recording unsuccessful as well as successful attempts. This produced a less dramatic story than the original demonstration, but a clearer account of what they did and did not yet understand.

Their supervisor also asked what they meant by an improvement. A filter that allowed water through rapidly might be attractive for one purpose, but speed alone did not show how well it removed unwanted material. The device had measured one property, not every property relevant to choosing a filter. The students had moved from a narrow observation to a broad recommendation without collecting the evidence that the recommendation required. They revised the claim so that its scope matched the measurement.

By exhibition day, the team could describe which parts of its procedure were consistent and which remained sensitive to small changes. Its display included the conflicting results from the other class. Some visitors found this surprising, expecting the presentation to celebrate an unambiguous discovery. The students explained that an independent attempt had revealed information they would otherwise have missed. Repetition was useful not merely when it confirmed a result, but also when disagreement exposed hidden assumptions or missing instructions.

The project did not prove that the new material was useless, nor did it establish a universal rule about which filter to choose. It demonstrated a more modest form of progress: turning a striking observation into a question that others could examine. The reliability of a conclusion depends partly on how clearly the path to it is described and how openly alternative explanations are considered. When a result refuses to repeat, the disagreement can become evidence about the investigation itself rather than simply an obstacle to announcing success.

questions.prompt: What omission was discovered when the classes compared procedures?
choices: The written instructions did not specify how firmly to fit the filters.
The instructions gave no information about which material was new.
The second class had not been told to record any measurements.
The original team had forgotten to mention that water was needed.
questions.explanationJa: 取り付ける際の押す強さが書かれておらず、二つのクラスの手順が実際には異なっていました。

evidence.quote: omitted the amount of pressure applied while fitting each filter

questions.prompt: Why did the students investigate further after discovering the pressure difference?
choices: They needed to prove that the second class had worked carelessly.
They had already eliminated every other explanation.
The difference suggested an explanation but did not establish it as the whole cause.
They wanted to remove unsuccessful attempts from the final display.

evidence.quote: did not establish that fitting pressure explained the entire difference

questions.prompt: Why did the supervisor question the meaning of “an improvement”?

To distinguish the measured property from the broader claim being made.
To suggest that unfamiliar materials are always inferior to familiar ones.
To explain why repeating the experiment was unnecessary.

evidence.quote: one property, not every property relevant to choosing a filter

paragraphs.text: When Emi joined her cousin's walking group, she expected everyone to discuss distance and speed. She had downloaded a phone application that counted every step, and she checked it whenever the group stopped. On the first Saturday, however, her cousin brought a notebook instead of a sports watch. The notebook contained drawings of leaves, old gates, and unusual clouds from previous walks.

Their route passed a narrow lane behind the shopping street. Emi wanted to hurry because the group was moving more slowly than she had expected. Then her cousin pointed to a small bird carrying grass into a hole in a wall. They stood quietly until it returned. Emi realized that she had walked through the lane many times without noticing that anything lived there.

At the next meeting, Emi suggested a longer route to a nearby hill. Several members liked the idea, but one person said she would prefer the flat path beside the canal. Rather than asking everyone to follow the hill route, the group chose a meeting place where the two routes ended. Members could select either route and still meet for conversation afterwards. No one had to explain why they preferred one path.

Emi continued using her application, but she stopped treating its number as the only reason to walk. She sometimes recorded a place she wanted to visit again or something interesting she had heard. For her, the walks became a welcome break from a busy week. She did not claim that the same routine would suit everybody. What mattered was finding an activity she enjoyed enough to continue, while leaving room for other people's different preferences.

paragraphs.text: After a winter storm, a large branch lay across the grass in Willow Garden. The path was clear, but the broken wood looked untidy. Haru, a new volunteer, offered to carry it away with the other fallen branches. Before he began, an older gardener named Rosa asked him to look carefully at its surface. Small insects were moving beneath the loose bark.

Rosa explained that the garden contained more than the flowers people came to photograph. Some living things used fallen wood as a place to hide or find food. She was not suggesting that every branch should remain exactly where it fell. Broken wood on a walking path could make the garden difficult to use. This branch, however, was resting in a corner where visitors did not normally walk.

Haru helped Rosa move it a short distance away from a young plant. They put up a small sign explaining why it had been left there. Over the following months, Haru drew the branch in his notebook. Its shape changed slowly, and different plants grew nearby. Not every visit produced something exciting to record. He learned that looking after a garden sometimes involved watching patiently rather than immediately changing what he saw.

When a visitor later complained about the corner, Haru listened instead of saying that she knew nothing about nature. She was worried that children might trip over the branch while playing. He showed her the nearby open area and explained the difference between the play space and the quieter corner. The conversation reminded him that a useful explanation should address the concern people actually have. Keeping the branch required both care for living things and attention to how people shared the garden.

paragraphs.text: Noah was confident that he could reach the museum without a car. The journey planner on his phone showed two buses and a short transfer between them. He allowed extra time and left home early. Yet when his first bus arrived in the town center, he could not find the stop for the second bus. The planner gave the same street name for both stops.

A driver explained that the next bus left from the opposite side of a busy road. Noah could see the shelter, but a fence prevented him from crossing directly. He had to walk to a crossing farther along the street and then walk back. By the time he reached the shelter, the second bus had gone. The transfer had been short on the map but longer on foot.

At the museum, Noah told his friend Lea about the experience. Lea used the route regularly and knew the crossing well. She had never thought of mentioning it when giving visitors directions. Together they wrote a short description for the museum's travel page. It included a photograph of the correct shelter and a clear instruction to use the crossing beside the supermarket. They also advised visitors to check the current bus times before leaving.

The description did not promise that connections would always work. Buses could still be delayed, and some visitors would need more time to walk between stops. Instead, it made a hidden part of the journey visible. Noah was pleased that his difficulty had led to something useful. He still used the planner, but now he paid closer attention to what happened between the lines on the screen. Reaching a destination meant more than knowing the names of the vehicles to board.

readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。

paragraphs.text: The drama club at Westbrook School was preparing a poster for its summer performance. A member found a beautiful photograph of an empty theater on the internet. There was no price beside the image, and it was easy to download. Several students assumed that they could use it simply because anyone could see it online. Their teacher asked them to check before printing the posters.

The students found the photographer's contact details and sent a message describing the performance. They explained how many posters they hoped to print and where the image would appear. The photographer replied that they could use the picture on twenty printed posters if they included her name. Her message did not mention putting it on the club's social media page.

One member suggested uploading the poster online as well, since the photographer had already agreed to help. Another student, Ren, pointed out that the reply covered a particular use. Rather than guessing, the club asked a second question. The photographer allowed the online use too, but requested a link to her website. The students saved both messages in the club's shared folder so that the next person preparing the poster could read the conditions.

For a later event, the club decided to take its own photographs. This gave members more control over the appearance of their materials, although they still discussed who would be photographed and how the images would be used. Ren thought the first poster had taught them a useful habit: describe a planned use clearly and keep a record of the answer. Finding a picture was only the beginning. Understanding the permission attached to it was a separate part of the task.

choices: Every photograph online had been taken by a professional.

readings.title: A Place at the Long Table
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Every autumn, the residents of Maple Court held a meal in their shared courtyard. Each household usually brought a dish, and the tables were pushed together to make one long line. When a new resident named Sam arrived with nothing to share, he stayed near the gate. He had just moved into the building and had not yet unpacked his kitchen equipment.

A neighbor invited Sam to sit down, but he felt uncomfortable taking food without contributing something. She explained that there were other ways to help. He could carry empty plates, tell people where to find water, or simply join a conversation. Sam began by bringing chairs from the storage room. Soon he was sitting beside an older resident who told him how the courtyard had changed over the years.

The following spring, Sam helped organize another meal. Remembering his first visit, he suggested changing the invitation. Instead of saying that everyone should bring a dish, it said that people were welcome whether or not they could bring food. A short list described optional jobs for anyone who wanted one. The organizers also left space at the end of the table for people who might decide to come after the meal had begun.

Not every resident attended. Some preferred to spend the evening quietly, and others had different plans. Sam did not treat their absence as a problem to solve. He wanted the invitation to make joining easier, not to make declining difficult. At the meal, he noticed a student standing near the gate and remembered how that had felt. He offered a seat without first asking what the student had brought. The table was a place to meet neighbors, not a test of what each person could provide.

readings.title: Which Friday?
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Lila sent her cousin Ben a short voice message on Sunday. She said, "Let's meet next Friday after lunch at the station." She thought the plan was clear and began looking forward to their visit to an art exhibition. Ben listened while cooking dinner. He replied that he was happy to come, but neither of them wrote the date down.

On the Friday that followed, Lila waited outside the station with two exhibition tickets. Ben was still at home. When she called, he explained that he had understood "next Friday" to mean the Friday of the following week. They were both surprised. Neither had intended to change the plan, and each had believed that the other understood it in the same way.

Lila was disappointed, but she avoided starting the conversation by accusing Ben of not listening. Instead, they compared what each had understood. They found that the words "after lunch" were also less precise than they had realized. Lila normally ate at noon, while Ben often finished lunch much later. They agreed to meet the following day and sent each other a written message with the full date, the time, and the station exit.

The next meeting went smoothly. Ben brought a small sketchbook, and they spent the afternoon drawing objects they liked in the exhibition. Later, Lila did not decide that voice messages were useless. She still used them to share stories or discuss ideas. For arrangements involving tickets and travel, however, she added a written summary and asked Ben to confirm it. She had learned that a message could sound friendly and familiar while still leaving important details open to more than one interpretation.

choices: Ben was unable to hear any part of the message.

readings.title: The Empty Box on the Form
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: When a fictional design studio introduced a voluntary wellbeing journal, Marta initially welcomed it. Employees could record activities they found restorative, from gardening to meeting a friend, and reflect on how they wanted to spend their time outside work. Marta liked the questions because they encouraged her to notice small pleasures rather than pursue an impressive target. She wrote about making soup with her father and listening to music on her journey home. The journal seemed to belong to her.

That impression changed when the studio began inviting employees to share a weekly summary. A notice said that participation remained voluntary, but team leaders asked who had completed the form at the end of each meeting. Colleagues often described long runs or demanding hikes. Marta, whose evenings also involved caring for a relative, started leaving out quieter activities. Nothing in the instructions required this. Nevertheless, she began shaping her account around what seemed likely to receive public approval.

A colleague named Daniel left the summary blank. When someone joked that he must have had an uneventful week, he explained that he preferred not to discuss his personal time at work. He did not oppose the journal or suggest that others should stop sharing. His objection concerned the assumption that an empty box indicated a failure to do something worthwhile. The box could equally reflect a decision about privacy, a busy week, or a dislike of this particular way of recording experience.

Their conversation prompted Marta to speak with the person coordinating the journal. Rather than asking for a list of approved activities, she described the difference between choosing to reflect and feeling expected to report. The coordinator removed the public completion question from meetings. Employees who wanted to exchange ideas could join an optional lunchtime conversation, while the journal itself remained private. No manager received a list of people who chose not to attend, and participation was kept separate from discussions of job performance.

The change did not make every employee enthusiastic. Some still found written reflection unhelpful, and others enjoyed discussing specific exercise goals. The coordinator resisted replacing the old routine with another single model of a successful week. Instead, employees could suggest activities or ignore the journal entirely. Marta returned to writing about cooking, without treating it as evidence that she had achieved a prescribed amount of relaxation. Daniel continued to leave his journal unused and joined colleagues for lunch when he wanted company.

The episode illustrates a tension in organized efforts to support wellbeing. An invitation can lose some of its freedom when people believe that declining it requires an explanation. That does not make shared activities inherently harmful, nor does it establish that private reflection benefits everyone. It suggests that the conditions surrounding an offer matter as much as its friendly wording. In this studio, protecting the choice not to participate helped preserve the difference between a personal resource and an additional performance expected by the workplace.

readings.title: An Orchard Without a Single Picture
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: When the town of Merrow inherited an abandoned orchard, the gift arrived with a photograph taken several decades earlier. Neat rows of fruit trees filled the image, and children stood beside baskets on an open lawn. The photograph quickly became the unofficial plan for restoring the site. Supporters imagined removing the tangled vegetation and recreating the familiar arrangement. To them, the picture offered a clear standard against which progress could be judged, as well as a connection with the town's past.

Iris, who had been asked to prepare a map of the land, found a more complicated place. Some old trees were still producing fruit, while others had become hollow or fallen. Between them were patches of scrub, shaded ground, and small open spaces. She also noticed that the photograph showed only one corner at one moment. It could not reveal what had grown outside the frame, which paths were muddy in winter, or how much work had been required to maintain the ordered appearance.

At a meeting, Iris did not argue that the photograph was worthless. It showed the orchard's former purpose and helped residents explain their attachment to it. However, she distinguished a historical record from a complete instruction for the future. Restoring fruit production, providing accessible paths, retaining sheltered areas for wildlife, and preserving every old tree were different aims. They might support one another in some places and conflict in others. Calling all of them restoration did not remove the need to make choices.

The group therefore discussed particular parts of the site rather than voting on a single image. Near the entrance, it proposed a clear route to a small gathering space. Farther away, some quieter areas would remain difficult to enter. A specialist assessment would guide decisions about damaged trees beside paths, rather than treating age alone as a reason to remove or retain them. Volunteers also considered who would look after newly planted trees after the first season of public enthusiasm had passed.

One disagreement remained over a line of young trees that had grown where an older row once stood. Removing them would make the historic layout easier to recognize. Keeping some would preserve the site's more recent changes. The eventual plan retained part of the line and used a drawing to show the former arrangement. A few residents found this unsatisfactory because the orchard would never look exactly like the photograph. Others valued the fact that its different periods would remain visible together rather than being reduced to one chosen date.

The orchard was not presented as a model that every community should copy. Its importance lay in how the group reconsidered its starting assumption. A landscape can carry memories without being frozen into a particular picture. Historical evidence, present conditions, and future responsibilities answer different questions, and none supplies a complete decision by itself. By making those questions explicit, the residents could explain both what they intended to preserve and what they were prepared to change, even when agreement remained incomplete.

choices: It served as an informal picture of what the restored orchard should become.
It showed that the town had no connection with the land.
It supplied a complete record of maintenance across several seasons.
It proved that fruit trees could no longer grow on the site.

readings.title: The Last Street of the Journey
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: By the time a parcel reached Bell Street, it had crossed a sea, passed through a regional depot, and traveled along a motorway. Yet the last few hundred meters could be the most unpredictable part of its journey. The narrow street contained apartments, a bakery, a repair shop, and a school entrance. At different hours, the same section of curb became a delivery space, a place to collect children, or a temporary stopping point for someone helping an older relative out of a car.

A transport planner named Joel first visited early one morning. The street appeared quiet, and he wondered why residents described it as constantly congested. He returned at midday and again before the school day ended. The visits revealed overlapping demands that were invisible in a map showing only the road's width. The bakery needed flour before its busiest working hours, while the repair shop received irregular deliveries of heavy parts. A uniform rule about when vehicles could stop would affect these activities in different ways.

One proposal would have moved all deliveries to a depot outside the center, with the final stage completed by small vehicles. Supporters emphasized the possibility of fewer large vans entering the street. A shopkeeper asked what would happen when a delivery missed the depot's departure time. Another pointed out that some goods could be carried easily in small loads, whereas a machine part might require different equipment. These questions did not establish that the proposal was impractical. They identified arrangements that would need to work before its benefits could be assumed.

Joel also spoke with a driver who knew the street well. The driver explained that a sign saying deliveries could stop for ten minutes did not create an available space. If the space was occupied, the driver had to wait elsewhere or return later. Time saved on the motorway could disappear while searching for somewhere to unload. For residents, meanwhile, a vehicle waiting with its engine running was not an abstract delay in a transport schedule. It was an interruption beside a bedroom window or a blocked view at the crossing.

The resulting discussion moved beyond the question of which vehicle was smallest. Participants considered different loading periods for different sections of the street, clearer information for occasional drivers, and ways for shops to combine orders when practical. No single arrangement could satisfy every urgent delivery and every resident at all times. The plan therefore included a contact point for reporting recurring conflicts, rather than assuming that publishing a timetable would settle them permanently. The school entrance remained a separate concern requiring attention to people crossing the road.

Bell Street's experience suggests why the final stage of transport cannot be understood simply as a shorter version of the earlier stages. Movement through a neighborhood involves access to limited shared space and coordination with activities that have their own timing. Efficient travel between distant locations remains valuable, but it does not automatically produce a smooth arrival. A useful account of a journey must include what happens when the vehicle stops, who needs the space then, and which practical burdens have been shifted rather than removed.

readings.title: What the Receipt Could Prove
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: The volunteer theater in Brookhaven had used a carved wooden screen in several productions when a former member asked for it back. She said that she had lent it for one summer performance. The current committee believed it had been donated. No one accused anyone else of dishonesty at first; the difficulty was that people remembered the original arrangement differently. The screen was now central to a forthcoming production, which made the uncertainty inconvenient without making either account more accurate.

The theater's own dispute procedure allowed an uninvolved volunteer to hear both sides and recommend a resolution. This was an internal arrangement, not a court process. The volunteer, Malik, began by separating the question of what had happened from the question of what the committee wished to happen now. Keeping the screen would save money, but that practical advantage did not establish ownership. Equally, the former member's disappointment did not by itself demonstrate that a temporary loan had been agreed.

A receipt seemed at first to settle the matter. It recorded that the theater had paid a transport company to collect the screen from the member's house. Several committee members regarded this as evidence of a permanent transfer. Malik pointed out that transport costs could have been paid for either a loan or a donation. The receipt supported one narrow claim: the theater had arranged and paid for collection. It did not contain the terms under which the object would remain there.

An old email added useful but incomplete information. It referred to using the screen "for the summer production," without stating what should happen afterwards. The committee had kept it in storage and used it again, while the former member had not contacted the theater for several years. Malik resisted treating the silence as decisive. It might reflect agreement, but it could also reflect distance, distraction, or an assumption that the screen was still being looked after. He invited both sides to comment on the documents before proposing any solution.

Eventually, they agreed that the theater would use the screen for its forthcoming performance and then return it on a stated date. The theater would cover the return transport. This compromise did not produce a conclusive account of the original conversation. Instead, it established an arrangement both sides were willing to accept now. Malik's written summary made that distinction clear so that future committee members would not mistake the agreement for proof that one version of the past had been established.

Afterwards, the theater adopted a simple record for objects arriving on loan or as gifts. It identified the item, the parties, any conditions, and who would keep a copy. The change could not guarantee that disputes would disappear, but it reduced reliance on assumptions surviving unchanged as volunteers came and went. The case illustrated two different tasks: assessing what evidence supports and designing a workable resolution. They can inform each other, yet a convenient outcome should not be presented as stronger evidence than the available records justify.

readings.title: Voices Missing from the Recording
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: While preparing an exhibition about a closed clothing factory, a community archivist named Lina found a box of recorded interviews. Former employees described friendships, practical jokes, and pride in making useful goods. Their voices were vivid enough to make the factory seem present again. A designer proposed playing the happiest extracts beside photographs of the final staff picnic. The exhibition could become a warm celebration of a workplace that had once connected many families in the town.

Lina valued those memories, but she noticed a pattern in the interview list. Most speakers had worked in the same department, and several had been introduced by one former supervisor. Workers from the evening shift were scarcely represented. Temporary employees appeared in photographs but had not been interviewed. The absence did not tell Lina what those people would have said. It did tell her that the surviving recordings could not simply stand for every experience of factory life.

She contacted several people whose names appeared in old staff notes. One former worker declined to participate because she did not want an argument from years earlier discussed publicly. Another was willing to talk but wanted parts concerning family members excluded. Lina respected those conditions. An archive could become broader without assuming that everyone owed it a complete personal history. She also kept a record of how the new interviews had been obtained, so later researchers could understand why some voices were easier to reach than others.

The additional conversations complicated rather than replaced the earlier accounts. A worker recalled enjoying the companionship of her colleagues while finding the changing shift schedule difficult. Someone else described learning valuable skills but feeling uncertain whenever a short contract approached its end. These were not necessarily corrections to the cheerful stories. Different experiences could coexist, and even one person could remember the same workplace with affection and frustration. Lina avoided arranging the display as a contest to decide whether the factory had been entirely good or entirely bad.

Instead, the exhibition placed short extracts around shared themes such as learning, working hours, and leaving. Each extract identified the speaker's role and the interview date, where permission allowed. A separate panel explained how the recordings had been selected and acknowledged gaps in the collection. Visitors could listen to longer sections rather than relying only on a sentence chosen for its emotional force. The final picnic photograph remained, but it no longer served as an uncomplicated summary of everything that had happened inside the factory.

The completed display was still selective. Space, available recordings, and the wishes of participants all limited what could be included. Lina did not claim to have removed those constraints or recovered every missing account. Her aim was to make the selection visible and prevent a vivid fragment from being mistaken for a complete social history. The exhibition preserved memories while also showing how they had reached the public, leaving visitors room to appreciate personal stories without assuming that the loudest or most accessible voices were the only ones that mattered.

questions.prompt: What could Lina reasonably conclude from the original interview list?
choices: Evening workers must have disliked the factory.
The first recordings represented only part of the workforce’s experience.
Temporary workers had never attended any factory events.
The supervisor had instructed every speaker to give a false account.
questions.explanationJa: 取材された人が特定の部署などに偏っていたため、工場全体の経験を代表するとは言えません。不在の人の意見そのものは分かりません。

evidence.quote: Lina respected those conditions.

evidence.quote: These were not necessarily corrections to the cheerful stories.

choices: To show that a complete history can be recovered from any small collection.

readings.title: Translating More Than a Word
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
readings.scenarioPolicy: 架空の人物・組織によるオリジナルの場面です。実在する研究・統計・時事報道の引用ではありません。

paragraphs.text: At a residents' meeting in the fictional town of Ashford, an interpreter named Nuri helped a newly arrived family discuss a proposed playground. The chair asked whether they could "support the project." Nuri translated the phrase, and the family agreed enthusiastically. A few minutes later, a volunteer passed them a form asking how much time they could contribute to construction. Their surprise revealed that the agreement had not meant the same thing to everyone in the room.

The family had understood support as approval of the idea. The volunteer had understood it as a willingness to help build the playground. Both meanings were plausible in the discussion, which had moved quickly from planning to practical arrangements. Nuri could have selected a more specific phrase, but she had not known which kind of support the chair intended. The difficulty was therefore not simply a missing equivalent between two languages. An ambiguity in the original question had been carried into the translated conversation.

Nuri paused the discussion and asked the chair to distinguish the two requests. Did the organizers want an opinion about the playground, an offer of time, or both? Once those questions were separated, the family could answer each one. They approved of the idea but could not promise construction work because of their working hours. They did offer to explain the plan to another family who had missed the meeting. This was a contribution the original form had not made easy to express.

After the meeting, someone suggested that Nuri should simply make all vague statements clearer while translating. She explained why this was not always possible. Choosing a specific meaning without checking could silently change what a speaker was asking or promising. At other times, a phrase might be deliberately broad because a decision had not yet been made. Her responsibility was not to settle the town's unfinished decisions on behalf of its speakers. When an ambiguity affected an important commitment, she needed room to ask for clarification.

The chair subsequently introduced a brief pause before asking participants to agree to a task. The exact request was stated, and anyone could explain a condition or ask a question. This helped residents using the same language as the chair as well as those relying on interpretation. The change did not require every casual remark to be defined with legal precision. It focused attention on moments when people were being asked to commit time, money, or responsibility, and where a mistaken assumption would matter later.

Nuri's experience shows that communication cannot always be repaired by replacing one word with a better word. Shared understanding may depend on distinguishing several intentions that a familiar expression has compressed together. A competent interpreter can make these difficulties visible, but cannot guarantee understanding if participants are unwilling to pause. In Ashford, the most useful change was permission to interrupt an apparently smooth conversation long enough to establish what agreement actually involved. The brief interruption protected a clearer choice instead of being treated as an obstacle to efficient discussion.

questions.prompt: How did the family initially understand “support the project”?
choices: As a requirement to pay for all construction materials.
As a promise to attend every future meeting.
As approval of the playground proposal.
As an invitation to become professional interpreters.
questions.explanationJa: 家族は計画への賛成という意味で受け取り、建設作業の約束とは考えていませんでした。

evidence.quote: The family had understood support as approval of the idea.

questions.prompt: Why could the problem not be attributed only to Nuri’s vocabulary choice?
choices: The chair’s original phrase itself left the intended commitment unclear.
The family had refused to listen to any translated explanation.
The meeting had already approved a detailed construction contract.
The volunteer knew that the family opposed the playground.
questions.explanationJa: 元のsupportにも複数の意味があり、司会が何を求めているか確認できていなかったためです。

evidence.quote: An ambiguity in the original question had been carried into the translated conversation.

questions.prompt: Why did Nuri reject the idea of silently making every vague statement specific?
choices: She thought all meetings should avoid practical decisions.
She believed participants preferred not to understand one another.
She was only willing to translate written forms.
Doing so could change a speaker’s intended request or promise.
questions.explanationJa: 確認なしに意味を限定すると、話し手の依頼や約束を通訳側が変更してしまう可能性があるためです。

evidence.quote: Choosing a specific meaning without checking could silently change what a speaker was asking or promising.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about clarification during discussion?
choices: It should be avoided whenever a conversation seems fluent.
A short pause can protect meaningful agreement about important commitments.
It is useful only when participants speak different languages.
It requires every informal comment to receive a formal definition.
questions.explanationJa: 滑らかな会話でも重要な約束の意味を確認する短い中断が必要なことがあります。同じ言語の参加者にも役立ちました。

evidence.quote: The brief interruption protected a clearer choice instead of being treated as an obstacle to efficient discussion.

readings.title: A Song with Room for the Listener
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Nora wrote a song for her school's autumn concert. It described someone standing at a station after a friend had left. Nora knew exactly who the friend was and why the journey mattered, but she did not put those details into the song. Instead, she described a cold bench, an unfinished cup of tea, and the sound of a departing train.

At the first rehearsal, her friend Ben asked whether the song was about moving to another country. A younger student thought it was about two people who had argued. Nora worried that she had failed to explain her story. She added a long verse telling the listener when the friendship began and what had happened before the departure.

The new verse answered the questions, but singing it felt awkward. The melody had to repeat several times to fit all the words. More importantly, Nora noticed that listeners now talked mostly about the events. Before the change, they had talked about moments in their own lives when they had wanted someone to stay. The extra details had made the story clearer while leaving less room for a personal response.

Nora removed most of the new verse. She kept one sentence that explained why the singer stayed on the platform, because without it the final action was confusing. At the concert, she did not introduce the song with its full background. Afterwards, Ben said it reminded him of saying goodbye to his brother. That was different from Nora's original experience, but she no longer treated the difference as a mistake. She had learned to distinguish information that helped listeners follow a song from information that merely made them share her exact interpretation.

questions.prompt: What did Nora initially leave out of her song?
choices: The sound heard at the station.
The personal history behind the departure.
The place where the singer was waiting.
The objects around the singer.
questions.explanationJa: 駅や物音などは描写しましたが、友人が誰で、なぜ旅が重要なのかという具体的な事情は入れませんでした。

evidence.quote: she did not put those details into the song

questions.prompt: Why did Nora first add another verse?
choices: She wanted to include a second singer.
She needed to make the concert last longer.
She hoped to remove all descriptions of the station.
She believed different interpretations showed that her story was unclear.
questions.explanationJa: 別々の解釈を聞き、自分の物語をうまく説明できていないと不安になったためです。

evidence.quote: Nora worried that she had failed to explain her story

questions.prompt: What did Nora notice after adding the verse?
choices: Listeners focused more on the events than on their own experiences.
The melody became shorter and easier to sing.
Nobody could understand where the song took place.
Listeners all remembered the same family member.
questions.explanationJa: 追加前は自分の体験を語っていた聴き手が、追加後は歌の出来事を中心に話すようになりました。

evidence.quote: listeners now talked mostly about the events

questions.prompt: What did Nora learn about explaining a song?
choices: Every listener should discover the writer’s complete history.
Removing every clear detail makes a song more effective.
Some clarity is useful without requiring one identical interpretation.
A song should change its meaning whenever anyone asks a question.
questions.explanationJa: 筋を追うために必要な説明は残しつつ、全員に自分と同じ解釈を求める必要はないと学びました。

evidence.quote: distinguish information that helped listeners follow a song from information that merely made them share her exact interpretation

readings.title: The Second Runner
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。

paragraphs.text: Daniel was the fastest runner in his class over a short distance. When the class prepared for a relay race, he expected to run the final section. He imagined crossing the finish line while everyone cheered. His teacher instead placed him second. Daniel was disappointed and asked whether she had forgotten his result from the individual race.

The teacher explained that choosing a relay team involved more than comparing separate running times. Daniel could receive the baton smoothly from a slower runner and pass it accurately to the next person. Another student, Luis, ran well when he could see someone ahead and chase them. The teacher wanted Luis to finish and Daniel to help connect the middle of the team.

At first, Daniel practiced his own running more than the exchanges. During a practice race, he started too early and left the first runner struggling to reach him. They lost several seconds. Daniel's individual section was still quick, but the team's total time was worse. He realized that leaving sooner was not helpful if his teammate could not complete the pass.

Before the next practice, the two runners agreed on a clear starting signal. Daniel also asked the third runner where she preferred to receive the baton. Their coordination improved, and the team finished faster even though Daniel did not set a personal record. On race day, Luis crossed the line just behind the winning team. Daniel was disappointed about losing, but he could also name things they had done well. Later, he kept a photograph of the second exchange rather than the finish. It showed an important part of the race that he had once thought nobody would notice.

questions.prompt: Why did the teacher choose Daniel for the second section?
choices: He was unable to run in front of a crowd.
He had asked to avoid competing against Luis.
His ability to exchange the baton suited that position.
His individual running time was the slowest.
questions.explanationJa: ダニエルは前後の走者と正確にバトンを受け渡すことができ、中間のつなぎ役に向いていたためです。

evidence.quote: receive the baton smoothly from a slower runner and pass it accurately to the next person

questions.prompt: What caused trouble during the first practice race?

Better coordination can help even without faster individual running.

readings.title: What the Recipe Left Out
readings.levelNote: 英検対策の学習目安です。公式問題・公式の級別認定・他試験とのスコア換算ではありません。
